prompt: What is the main purpose of the acceleration lane at a freeway entrance?
choices: To let you pass slower vehicles on the ramp
To give you a place to stop and wait for traffic to clear
To let freeway drivers leave the freeway early
To let you reach freeway speed before merging
explanation: An acceleration lane runs beside the main lanes so you can reach the speed of freeway traffic before merging. It also lets freeway drivers see you before you enter.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 56, FL p. 71, AL p. 78)

prompt: When you merge onto a freeway from an entrance ramp, who has the right-of-way?
choices: Vehicles already traveling on the freeway
The vehicle entering from the ramp, if it signals
Whichever vehicle is larger
Whichever vehicle is moving faster
explanation: Drivers entering a freeway must yield to traffic already on it. Merge only when there is a safe gap.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 29, TX p. 53, CO p. 17)

prompt: At about what speed should you try to join freeway traffic from the acceleration lane?
choices: Well below the speed of traffic, to be cautious
At or near the speed of freeway traffic
Much faster than traffic, so you can get ahead of it
The speed you were driving on the ramp curve
explanation: Use the acceleration lane to reach the speed of freeway traffic. Merging much slower forces freeway drivers to brake, and merging much faster makes it hard to fit into a gap.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NV p. 36, CA p. 29, PA p. 50)

prompt: You are in the acceleration lane and want to merge. Which order of steps is safest?
choices: Stop at the end of the lane, then look for traffic
Merge first, then signal once you are in the lane
Signal, find a gap, match speed, then merge
Signal and move over right away, since freeway drivers must make room
explanation: Signal early, find a gap using your mirrors and a head check, adjust your speed to the traffic, and merge smoothly. Freeway drivers do not have to make room for you.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 50, FL p. 71, CA p. 29)

prompt: Why should you avoid stopping in an acceleration lane unless it is absolutely necessary?
choices: Stopping there makes the ramp meter reset
Freeway drivers would then be required to stop and let you in
A stopped car in that lane is treated as a breakdown
You would have to enter fast traffic from a standstill
explanation: A stop in the acceleration lane means you must enter fast-moving traffic from a standstill, and drivers behind you may not expect you to stop. Keep moving and adjust your speed to find a gap.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NV p. 36, AK p. 70, CA p. 29)

prompt: You reach a short freeway entrance with a YIELD sign and no acceleration lane. Traffic is heavy. What is the safest way to enter?
choices: Stop if needed and wait for a large gap
Keep rolling and squeeze in, because freeway traffic must let you in
Drive along the shoulder to build up speed first
Merge slowly at ramp speed and let freeway drivers brake for you
explanation: Without an acceleration lane you cannot reach freeway speed before merging, so obey the YIELD sign, stop if necessary, and wait for a gap big enough to enter and accelerate.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 62, AL p. 78-79)

prompt: A solid white line separates the entrance lane from the freeway lanes for a short distance. When may you merge?
choices: As soon as you reach freeway speed, even across the solid line
After the solid line ends, when you have a safe gap
Any time, as long as your turn signal is on
Only after the entrance lane has completely ended
explanation: Do not cross the solid white line while merging; wait until it ends. Waiting until the lane fully ends is also wrong because it leaves you no room to adjust.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 17, CA p. 29)

prompt: You are driving in the right lane of a freeway and see a car on the entrance ramp trying to merge. What is the best thing to do?
choices: Speed up to close the gap, since you have the right-of-way
Brake to a stop in your lane so the car can enter
If safe, move left or adjust speed to make room
Hold your speed and position and sound your horn
explanation: Even though the merging driver must yield, freeway drivers should help when they safely can by changing lanes or adjusting speed. Stopping on the freeway creates a new hazard.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 64, NE p. 68, FL p. 72)

prompt: What is the purpose of a ramp meter at a freeway entrance?
choices: To space out vehicles entering the freeway
To measure the speed of entering vehicles for speeding tickets
To show how far it is to the next exit
To warn drivers about wrong-way vehicles
explanation: Ramp meters are traffic signals on entrance ramps that release vehicles onto busy freeways at a controlled rate, usually during rush hours.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 12, CO p. 17, NV p. 36)

prompt: A ramp meter on the entrance ramp is turned on and showing red. What should you do?
choices: Slow down and continue, since ramp meters are only advisory
Treat it like a yield sign and go if the freeway looks clear
Stop at the stop line and wait for the green light
Drive around the waiting cars on the shoulder
explanation: When a ramp meter is operating you must stop at the line on red and wait for green before continuing onto the freeway.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NV p. 36, CO p. 17, PA p. 12)

prompt: The ramp meter turns green for you. What does the green light mean?
choices: Freeway traffic must now yield to you
You must merge immediately, wherever you are on the ramp
You and the car behind you may both enter on this green
You may go, but must still yield to freeway traffic
explanation: A green ramp meter only releases you onto the ramp. It does not protect your entry, so you must still look for a safe gap and yield to traffic on the freeway.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 12, NV p. 36)

prompt: A sign next to a ramp meter says ONE CAR PER GREEN. The car ahead of you just went on the green. What should you do?
choices: Follow closely behind the car ahead before the light changes
Stop at the line and wait for the next green light
Go if you can see a gap on the freeway
Sound your horn so the driver ahead moves faster
explanation: Ramp meters release a set number of vehicles per green, often one. Wait for your own green; the signals cycle faster than at a normal intersection.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NV p. 36-37, PA p. 12)

prompt: When leaving a freeway, where should you begin to slow down?
choices: Once you are in the exit lane
In the freeway travel lane, before the exit lane starts
As soon as you see the first sign for your exit
Only when you reach the end of the exit ramp
explanation: Keep your speed while on the freeway and slow down once you are in the deceleration lane. Slowing in the travel lane can cause rear-end crashes.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 56, NV p. 40, CO p. 18)

prompt: You just drove past the freeway exit you wanted. What should you do?
choices: Stop on the shoulder and back up to the exit
Make a U-turn through the median
Cut across the painted area to reach the ramp
Go on to the next exit
explanation: Never stop, back up, or cross the median on a freeway. Take the next exit and come back.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 56, AL p. 80, NJ p. 71)

prompt: When should you move into the lane you need for your freeway exit?
choices: At the last moment, so you don't hold up traffic
Only once the exit ramp begins
Well before the exit
After you pass the last sign for the exit
explanation: Plan ahead and get into the proper lane early. The heavier the traffic, the earlier you should move over to avoid a last-second lane change.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 56, NE p. 68, TX p. 54)

prompt: Your exit is one mile ahead, but you are three lanes away from the exit lane. What should you do?
choices: Cross all three lanes in one smooth movement
Change lanes one at a time, checking each time
Slow down in your lane until gaps open in all three lanes
Wait until you are near the exit, then cut across quickly
explanation: Move over one lane at a time and signal and check your blind spot each time. Crossing several lanes at once or swerving at the last second is dangerous.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 29, PA p. 56)

prompt: You have just left a freeway after driving a long time. What should you do now?
choices: Check your speed and watch for two-way traffic
Keep your freeway speed until you see a speed limit sign
Use the same following distance you used on the freeway
Speed up, since local roads have lower crash risks
explanation: Roads off the freeway usually have lower speed limits and may carry two-way traffic, cross streets, and pedestrians. Check your speedometer to make sure you have slowed enough.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 62, NE p. 69)

prompt: You realize you have taken the wrong exit and are now on the exit ramp. What should you do?
choices: Stop on the ramp and back up onto the freeway
Turn around on the ramp and drive back up it
Stop on the ramp to look up directions
Continue off the ramp and find your way back
explanation: Do not stop or back up on a ramp; stopped cars there are a major cause of rear-end crashes. Leave the freeway, figure out your route, and get back on if needed.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AK p. 70, NY p. 62)

prompt: Your exit is on the LEFT side of the freeway. How should you prepare?
choices: Stay in the right lane, since left exits are only for trucks
Wait in the right lane and cross over at the last moment
Move into the left lane well before the exit
Slow down in the right lane until the exit appears
explanation: Most exits are on the right, but some are on the left. Signs tell you which lane to use, so read them early and move over in advance.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 71, FL p. 72)

prompt: What is a cloverleaf interchange?
choices: A traffic circle built at the same level as the freeway
An interchange that uses loop-shaped ramps
An intersection on the freeway controlled by traffic lights
A rest area with its own entrance and exit ramps
explanation: A cloverleaf uses loop-shaped ramps to let traffic turn on or off the freeway in all directions without left turns across traffic.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AL p. 79, NJ p. 74)

prompt: In a weave lane, where entering and exiting traffic share the same short lane, who should yield?
choices: The driver leaving the freeway yields to the one entering
The driver entering the freeway yields to the driver leaving it
The driver on the left yields to the driver on the right
The slower vehicle always has the right-of-way
explanation: When drivers entering and exiting want the same space in a weave lane, the driver entering the freeway must yield to the driver who is exiting.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 72, PA p. 56)

prompt: How should you drive through the tight loop ramp of a cloverleaf interchange?
choices: Keep freeway speed so merging is easier at the end
Speed up in the curve to hold your lane
Stop at the start of the loop to check for traffic
Slow down to the posted ramp speed before the curve
explanation: Loop ramps are sharp curves. Watch for the entrance and exit signs and drive slowly through the loop, obeying the posted speed.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 74, PA p. 56)

prompt: Why should you avoid weaving from lane to lane on a freeway?
choices: It increases the chance of a crash and rarely saves much time
It is the only way to keep up with the flow of traffic
It helps you avoid other drivers' blind spots
It lowers the chance of being rear-ended
explanation: Lane hopping is dangerous, annoys other drivers, and seldom gets you there faster. Pick a lane and stay in it as much as possible.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NV p. 36, CA p. 21, TX p. 54)

prompt: Rear-end collisions are a leading danger on freeways. What is the best way to avoid one?
choices: Follow closely so other drivers cannot cut in front of you
Keep a safe following distance and look far ahead
Watch only the car directly in front of you
Use the left lane at all times
explanation: Following too closely and not paying attention cause most freeway rear-end crashes. Leave space and scan far ahead so you can slow down gradually.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., FL p. 73, PA p. 56)

prompt: When is it acceptable to stop on a freeway or its shoulder?
choices: To let a passenger get out
To check a map or your phone, if you use the shoulder
Only in an emergency or when police direct you
When you have missed your exit
explanation: Do not stop in freeway travel lanes or on the shoulder except for an emergency or when an officer tells you to. Keep moving until you can safely leave the freeway.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 35, FL p. 72, MT p. 47)

prompt: What is "highway hypnosis"?
choices: A dizzy feeling caused by looking at bright headlights
Feeling nervous when merging into fast traffic
Losing track of your speed after leaving the freeway
A drowsy, trance-like state from long, dull driving
explanation: Steady engine and tire noise and an unchanging view can lull a driver into a trance-like state where they stop actively scanning the road.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 58, TX p. 54, AL p. 34)

prompt: Which habit best helps you avoid highway hypnosis on a long drive?
choices: Stare at the lane line ahead
Keep your eyes moving and check your mirrors
Set cruise control and relax your attention
Drive faster so the trip ends sooner
explanation: Highway hypnosis comes from staring straight ahead too long. Keep shifting your gaze, read signs, check mirrors, and take regular breaks.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 94, TX p. 54, AL p. 34)

prompt: Which of these is a warning sign that you are too tired to drive safely?
choices: You can't remember driving the last few miles
You feel alert right after a rest stop
You notice more road signs than usual
You keep a steady lane position
explanation: Signs of fatigue include memory gaps, yawning, heavy eyelids, drifting between lanes, missing signs, and hitting rumble strips.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 51, NE p. 74)

prompt: On a long freeway trip you keep yawning and your tires just hit the rumble strip. What should you do?
choices: Open the windows and turn up the radio until you feel alert
Drink an energy drink and keep going
Speed up so you arrive before you get more tired
Get off at the next safe place and rest
explanation: Yawning and hitting the rumble strip mean you are drowsy, and the real fix is to stop and rest. The radio, an open window or an energy drink may help for a moment, but they do not replace sleep.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AL p. 34, NE p. 74, AZ p. 58)

prompt: Which statement about coffee, energy drinks, or "stay-awake" pills on a long drive is correct?
choices: They fully restore alertness
They are a safe way to drive through the night
They may help briefly, but they do not replace sleep
They work better than stopping to rest
explanation: Stimulants may mask tiredness for a short time, but they do not replace sleep, and stay-awake pills can make your driving even more hazardous. If you are drowsy, stop and rest.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NE p. 74, AL p. 34, GA p. 8)

prompt: Your car starts to break down while you are driving on a freeway. What should you do first?
choices: Stop in your lane and turn off the engine
Stop in the next lane to the left
Keep driving at freeway speed to the next exit
Signal and steer onto the shoulder, out of traffic
explanation: Get your vehicle completely off the travel lanes if you can. A stopped car in a freeway lane is very likely to be hit.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 75, NJ p. 73, TX p. 54)

prompt: After pulling onto the shoulder with a disabled vehicle, which lights should you turn on so other drivers can see you?
choices: Your high-beam headlights, so drivers see you from far away
Your hazard (emergency) flashers
Your left turn signal only
Your interior dome light only
explanation: Hazard flashers warn approaching drivers that your vehicle is stopped or disabled.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 18, NJ p. 73, TX p. 54)

prompt: Your car is disabled on the right shoulder of a busy freeway and you must get out. What is the safest way?
choices: Get out on the driver's side and stand behind the car to warn traffic
Stand in front of the car so passing drivers can see you
Get out on the side away from traffic
Walk along the edge of the travel lane to find help
explanation: If you must leave the car, exit on the side away from traffic and keep away from moving vehicles. Never stand behind or beside a disabled car next to traffic.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 75, TX p. 54)

prompt: You see a disabled vehicle on the freeway shoulder ahead with people standing near it. What should you do?
choices: Slow down and give it extra space
Keep your speed, since the vehicle is not in your lane
Stop behind it to see if you can help
Sound your horn as you pass to warn the people
explanation: Reduce speed and increase the space between you and a disabled vehicle. Watch for people, tow trucks, and police nearby.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 73, CA p. 64)

prompt: You get a flat tire while driving in the left lane of a busy freeway. What is the best action?
choices: Brake hard and stop in the lane to change the tire
Stop in the lane and turn on your hazard flashers
Keep driving at freeway speed until you reach the next exit
Slow gradually and steer off the travel lanes
explanation: Never stop in a travel lane if you can avoid it. A car with a flat can be driven slowly off the road; slow down gradually and work your way onto the shoulder.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., MT p. 47, TX p. 54, CA p. 74)

prompt: You are about to turn onto a freeway ramp and see DO NOT ENTER and WRONG WAY signs. What do they mean?
choices: The ramp is closed for construction only at night
Only trucks may use the ramp
You would be driving against traffic
You may enter but must yield to vehicles leaving the freeway
explanation: Freeway exit ramps are marked with DO NOT ENTER and WRONG WAY signs. Entering one puts you head-on with exiting traffic.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 56, NV p. 36)

prompt: Driving on a freeway at night, you notice the reflectors on the lane lines are glowing red in your headlights. What does this mean?
choices: The road ahead is closed
You are going the wrong way
You are approaching an exit
You are driving in a carpool lane
explanation: Pavement reflectors show red to drivers going the wrong way. If you see red reflectors facing you, you are headed against traffic.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 44, FL p. 73)

prompt: You turn onto a ramp and immediately see DO NOT ENTER and WRONG WAY signs facing you. What should you do?
choices: Back out or turn around when it is safe
Continue onto the freeway and look for a median crossing
Drive forward slowly with your hazard flashers on
Stop where you are and wait for police to arrive
explanation: This is the exception to the rule against backing up on a ramp: if you have entered a road the wrong way, back out or turn around as soon as it is safe rather than drive against traffic.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., FL p. 73, CA p. 44)

prompt: You are entering a divided highway on a ramp. Which pavement markings confirm you are going the correct direction?
choices: A white line on your left and a yellow line on your right
Yellow lines on both sides of your lane
Red reflectors facing you on the lane lines
A yellow line on your left and a white line on your right
explanation: On a divided highway, the yellow edge line is on your left and the white edge line is on your right when you travel the correct way.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 56)

prompt: On a divided freeway you see headlights coming straight toward you in your lanes. What should you do?
choices: Flash your lights and hold your lane
Slow down, steer away from it, then call 911 when safe
Brake hard and stop in your lane
Speed up to get past the vehicle quickly
explanation: Ease off the gas, make sure no one is next to you, and steer away from the wrong-way driver. When you reach a safe place, report it to 911.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 58)

prompt: On a freeway, in which lane are wrong-way drivers most often found?
choices: The far right lane, near the exit ramps they came from
The shoulder
The far left lane (or the HOV lane)
The exit lane
explanation: Wrong-way drivers usually travel in the left or HOV lane, and most are impaired. Be extra alert in the left lane, especially late at night.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 58)

prompt: What is the safest way to pass a large truck on a multi-lane highway?
choices: Pass on the left without lingering beside it
Pass on the right, where the driver can see you best
Stay beside the truck's cab until the driver waves you on
Pass on the shoulder if the lanes are full
explanation: Trucks have large blind spots along both sides. Pass on the left and complete the pass without staying alongside.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AL p. 29, NJ p. 151-152)

prompt: After passing a large truck, when is it safe to move back into its lane?
choices: When your back bumper clears its front bumper
As soon as you are past the truck's cab
When the truck driver sounds the horn
When you see the whole truck front in your rearview mirror
explanation: Cutting in too soon leaves the truck no room to stop. Wait until the whole front of the truck shows in your rearview mirror, then don't slow down.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NV p. 63, TX p. 57, NJ p. 151)

prompt: You are driving next to a large truck and cannot see the driver's face in the truck's side mirror. What does this mean?
choices: The truck driver probably cannot see you
The truck driver can see you clearly
The truck is about to slow down
You are at a safe distance from the truck's blind spots
explanation: If you can't see the driver in the truck's mirror, you are in a blind spot (no-zone). Speed up or drop back so you can be seen.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NV p. 62, AL p. 29, AK p. 82)

prompt: You want to pass a large truck on a long downhill grade. What should you expect?
choices: The truck will slow sharply, making the pass easier
It may speed up, so the pass can take longer
The truck must move to the shoulder to let you pass
Passing a truck downhill takes less time than on level ground
explanation: On a downgrade a truck's momentum can make it go faster, so you may need more speed and time to pass. On an upgrade trucks often lose speed and are easier to pass.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 57, PA p. 60)

prompt: A large truck is passing you on the highway. How can you help?
choices: Speed up so the truck can't pass
Move toward the truck to shorten its pass
Keep to the far side of your lane
Brake hard so the truck gets by faster
explanation: Stay on the far side of your lane and ease off slightly so the truck can complete its pass. Never speed up while a truck is passing you.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 57, PA p. 61)

prompt: A large truck passes close to your car at highway speed and its wind blast hits your vehicle. What should you do?
choices: Grip the wheel firmly and keep your lane position
Steer toward the truck to fight the wind
Brake hard until the truck is gone
Steer away onto the shoulder
explanation: Air turbulence from a large vehicle can push your car sideways. Hold the wheel firmly and keep space between you and the truck.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 57, NJ p. 152)

prompt: You are approaching a highway work zone. What should you do?
choices: Keep your normal speed if you don't see workers right away
Change lanes often to get through the zone faster
Follow the car ahead closely so you don't hold up traffic
Slow down and watch for workers and equipment
explanation: Work zones have changing lanes, workers, and equipment. Slow down, stay focused, and follow all signs and flagger directions.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 21, NJ p. 73)

prompt: What is the most common type of crash in highway work zones?
choices: Head-on collisions
Rear-end collisions
Rollovers on the shoulder
Collisions with parked construction equipment
explanation: Most work zone crashes are rear-end collisions. Watch the vehicle in front of you, leave extra space, and be ready to stop suddenly.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 21)

prompt: You see signs for a toll plaza ahead on the highway. What should you do?
choices: Keep your highway speed until you can see the booth lanes
Speed up to get into the shortest line first
Slow down early and watch for backed-up traffic
Stop on the shoulder to find your payment
explanation: Traffic may be backed up at toll booths. Slow down early and look for signs or lights that show which lanes are open.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 73)

prompt: You realize you have entered the wrong lane at a toll plaza. What should you do?
choices: Back up carefully and choose another lane
Continue through that lane
Stop and get out to ask an attendant for help
Swerve into the next lane at the last moment
explanation: Backing up or turning around at a toll plaza is dangerous. Stay in the lane and continue through it, staying inside your vehicle.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NH p. 31)

prompt: What should you do as you leave a toll booth?
choices: Watch both sides for merging cars and speed up smoothly
Accelerate hard to get ahead of the other cars
Stay in your lane; others must yield to you
Stop past the booth to put away your payment
explanation: After a toll booth, lanes often narrow and vehicles from other booths merge together. Search both sides and accelerate smoothly.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 73, NM p. 25)

prompt: What are electronic toll lanes designed to do?
choices: Let any vehicle skip the toll
Give emergency vehicles a place to park
Let drivers with a toll account pay without stopping
Check whether drivers are wearing seat belts
explanation: Electronic toll collection lets drivers with a transponder or toll account drive through designated lanes without stopping to pay cash. Obey the posted speed in those lanes.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NH p. 31, NJ p. 73)

prompt: An HOV or express lane is separated from the regular lanes by double solid white lines. How should you enter or leave it?
choices: Anywhere, as long as you signal first
Anywhere, if no vehicles are close behind you
Only by crossing the lines quickly at freeway speed
Only at marked openings in the lines
explanation: Never change lanes across double solid white lines. Use the designated entry and exit points for HOV and express lanes.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 20-21)
